sections.h2: Where is Habersham County and what lies inside it?
sections.html:
Habersham County fills a corner of northeast Georgia in the Blue Ridge, with Clarkesville as its seat and Cornelia as its biggest city. The legislature created it on December 15, 1818, and the name honors Colonel Joseph Habersham of the Continental Army. The county makes up the Cornelia, GA micropolitan statistical area (Wikipedia).

The county measures 279 square miles, 277 of them land, and part of the Chattahoochee National Forest lies within it. The high point is a knob of about 4,400 feet near the summit of Tray Mountain, a peak the county shares with White and Towns counties, and the Appalachian Trail follows the ridge close by. The Chattahoochee River rises in what used to be Habersham County, a point Sidney Lanier's poem about the river makes with its line about the hills of Habersham.

Habersham once spread across much of northeast Georgia. White and Lumpkin counties took land from it in 1857, Banks County in 1859 and Stephens County in 1905. Rabun, Stephens, Banks, Hall, White and Towns counties now touch it, along with Oconee County, South Carolina. Raoul is a census-designated place, and Batesville, Habersham Mills, Hollywood and Turnerville are unincorporated communities. One district, the Habersham County School District, serves the whole county, and Tallulah Falls School, Piedmont University and North Georgia Technical College are also found here.

sections.h2: What do the Census figures say about Habersham County homes?
sections.html:
At the 2020 census the county had 46,031 residents, and the July 2025 estimate of 50,416 is 9.5% higher. People aged 65 and up are 20.3% of the total, and 9.4% of residents were born abroad.

The assessors value each parcel as of January 1 using recent sales and market conditions, which is why a house's figure can shift when neighborhood sales do (QuickFacts).

sections.h2: Which Habersham County offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
The tax commissioner is an elected office created by the state constitution, and its job is billing, collecting, accounting for and paying out ad valorem tax. It has no say over values or millage rates. Values come from the Board of Tax Assessors, a five-member board created in 1968 as a three-member panel and expanded in 1990, with terms of three years. Millage rates come from the county commissioners and the school board, and the state's own levy cannot top one-fourth of one mill.

  • Tax commissioner: 130 Jacobs Way, Suite 202, Clarkesville, GA 30523, phone (706) 839-0120, Monday through Friday from 8:00 to 4:45, with Saturday service closed until further notice.
  • Tax assessors: phone (706) 839-0100, the number the county gives for mobile home registration questions.
  • Board of Tax Assessors meetings: second and fourth Mondays of the month, beginning at 9 a.m.

The commissioner's information page and the assessors' board page carry the details.

sections.h2: What dates matter on a Habersham County tax bill?
sections.html:
Habersham mails bills by August 15, and payment is expected by November 15 of the same year. That sits earlier than the December 20 default the state gives local governments leave to move. Mobile and modular homes run on another schedule: bills usually go out around February 1 and the tax and location permit are tied to April 1.

An owner who skips the April 1 payment and permit risks a 10% penalty, a citation to Habersham County Magistrate Court or a possible sale of the home. Owners must display the decal, and registration takes place at the assessors' office.

sections.h2: How does a Habersham County assessment appeal proceed?
sections.html:
Notices of assessment usually reach owners in spring, and a dissatisfied owner has 45 days from the notice date to respond. Grounds include taxability, value, uniformity or a denied exemption. The appeal is written, goes first to the Board of Tax Assessors and has to state which route you have chosen.

For mobile homes the county adds a second step: when the owner still disagrees after a changed value, an appeal to the Board of Equalization can be filed within 21 days of that notice. The grand jury appoints that board, whose job is to hear administrative appeals of assessors' values. The assessors' office can supply forms and the exact steps for a regular parcel.

sections.h2: What exemptions and special assessments exist in Habersham County?
sections.html:
Homestead applications are filed with the Tax Assessor's office, and first-time homeowners are told to bring a copy of the warranty deed. April 1 is the cutoff for the year you first claim, and later filings count for the next year. Approval renews itself until residence, ownership or the type you qualify for changes. The county says it has local exemptions that replace the state ones whenever the local amount is higher.

  • Bona fide agricultural property can be assessed at 30% rather than 40% of fair market value.
  • Conservation Use valuation depends on a covenant with the Board of Tax Assessors to keep the land in its qualifying use for at least 10 years.
  • Freeport exemption for manufacturers covers raw goods, goods in process and finished goods stored for shipment out of state, with applications from January 1 to April 1.
  • Equipment, machinery and fixtures of a business are assessed at 40% of fair market value.

sections.h2: What should a Habersham County seller do when tax is still due?
sections.html:
Georgia places the full year's bill on whoever owned the property on January 1, and the state gives no refund for part of a year. The contract of sale usually decides who pays what, so the first task is learning the exact balance.

Phone the tax commissioner at (706) 839-0120 and ask what is owed on the parcel for this year and any earlier ones. If closing falls between the August mailing and the November 15 deadline, tell the closing agent whether the new bill has been issued and paid. A mobile home bill follows the April 1 cycle and is separate from real property. A homestead exemption ends with a move or a change of ownership, so notify the assessors after you leave, and let the buyer file under their own name.

faqs.q: What day is Habersham County property tax due?
faqs.a: November 15 is the expected payment date, with bills mailed by August 15. Mobile and modular home bills usually go out around February 1, and that tax is tied to April 1.

faqs.q: Where do I find the Habersham County tax commissioner?
faqs.a: The Main Office is at 130 Jacobs Way, Suite 202, in Clarkesville, GA 30523. Call (706) 839-0120. Hours are Monday through Friday from 8:00 to 4:45, and Saturday service is closed until further notice.

faqs.q: What is the time limit to appeal a Habersham County value?
faqs.a: Forty-five days from the date printed on the assessment notice. Send a written appeal to the Board of Tax Assessors that states the method you choose.

faqs.q: By when must a Habersham County homestead application arrive?
faqs.a: April 1 of the first year you claim it. File with the Tax Assessor's office and bring your warranty deed if you recently bought the home.

faqs.q: Is farmland taxed differently in Habersham County?
faqs.a: Qualifying agricultural property can be assessed at 30% of fair market value instead of 40%. Conservation Use valuation applies current-use value and needs a covenant of at least 10 years with the Board of Tax Assessors.
